title: Watershed development in Ralegan Siddhi, Ahmadnagar, Maharashtra
body: Ralegan Siddhi is a small village in Ahmadnagar district, Maharashtra, that has become an example of watershed development for the whole country. In 1975 it was trapped in poverty and illicit liquor trade. Change began when a retired army man settled there and took up watershed development. He persuaded villagers to accept family planning and voluntary labour, and to stop open grazing, tree felling and liquor. Voluntary labour kept dependence on government financial aid to a minimum; in his words, it socialised the costs of the projects. Work began with the village percolation tank, whose leaking embankment the people repaired themselves; the seven wells below it filled with water in summer for the first time in living memory. A youth group, Tarun Mandal, worked against dowry, caste discrimination and untouchability. Open grazing was banned in favour of stall-feeding, the water-intensive crop sugarcane was banned, and pulses, oilseeds and low-water cash crops were encouraged. Today water is adequate and agriculture is flourishing, though the use of fertilisers and pesticides is very high, and people wonder whether the next generation can carry the work forward.
